questions.stem: A 24-year-old man attended outpatient clinic for initiation of ART after a recent diagnosis of HIV infection. He was keen to get started on treatment. Investigations: CD4 count 450 cells/μ L HIV RNA 120,000 copies/mL No baseline resistance demonstrated on HIV genotyping HLA B*5701 negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate antiretroviral regimen?
questions.explanation: Tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine + boosted darunavir Rilpivirine is not recommended in patients who have a HIV RNA >100,000 copies/mL or CD 4 T cell count <200 cells/μL at the start of treatment. Similarly abacavir is only recommended for treatment in patients with HIV RNA >100,000 copies/per mL if it is combined with dolutegravir. In practice INSTI-based regimens are preferred and NNRTI-based regimens are now considered alternative. However if an INSTI cannot be used then boosted darunavir, rilpivirine or efavirenz can be considered in combination with TDF or TAF .
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q35

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of myalgia of the lower extremities spreading proximally, increased fatigue, and polyuria. He was known to be HIVpositive, on treatment with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/ emtricitabine + raltegravir for the past year. Investigations: Sodium 135 mmol/L Potassium 2.0 mmol/L Glucose 90 mg/dl Chloride 107 mmol/L Bicarbonate 17 mEq/L Phosphorus 1.4 mg/dl Creatinine kinase 2015 U/L Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (previous baseline 1.2 mg/dL) Urinalysis: protein 30 mg/d and glucose 500 mg/dL Baseline genotype prior to initiating ART did not demonstrate resistance HLA B*5701 negative HBsAg positive
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment regimen?
questions.explanation: Abacavir/lamivudine/dolutegravir + entecavir The presence of a hyperchloremic nonanion gap metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, glucosuria, and proteinuria suggest that this patient has tenofovir-induced Fanconi’s syndrome; therefore tenofovir should be discontinued. Although raltegravir has been associated with rhabdomyolysis the other laboratory findings are suggestive of Fanconi’s syndrome. This patient has hepatitis B co-infection, and therefore an optimal treatment regimen should cover both viruses. Discontinuation of agents with anti-HBV activity can result in serious hepatocellular damage following reactivation of HBV . Lamivudine has activity against HBV; however, resistance develops quickly, and therefore dual therapy is recommended.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q36

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man attended for review. He was known to have hypertension, chronic hepatitis B, and HIV . He had been started 3 months earlier on lisinopril 10 mg daily and rosuvastatin 20 mg daily as he had an elevated Framingham risk score due to elevated blood pressure and hypercholesterolemia. He was also taking hydrochlorothiazide, aspirin, multivitamins, and elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide fumarate. Investigations: CD4 count 756 cells/μL HIV viral load undetectable 3 Months Earlier Current Visit Total cholesterol (mg/dL) 315 200 LDL (mg/dL) 197 80 HDL (mg/dL) 30 35 Triglycerides (mg/dL) 378 215 Total bilirubin (mg/dL) 0.9 1.1 Alkaline phosphatase (U/L) 45 46 ALT 34 116 AST 30 205
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of the new onset hepatitis?
questions.explanation: Drug–drug interaction with statin This patient is suffering from a drug–drug interaction from being on an antiretroviral therapy regimen with cobicistat and initiation of a statin. Because of the association of HIV with dyslipidemia, it is recommended to screen all new patients for hyperlipidemia at their first HIV Clinic appointment. If hyperlipidemia is found, then statins should be initiated, and lipid panels should be monitored within 1–3 months and then every 6–12 months thereafter. However, guidelines for initiation of a cholesterol-lowering agent are the same as the general population for persons living with HIV . It is contraindicated to start statins metabolized by CYP3A in patients on protease inhibitors, including simvastatin and lovastatin. For patients on a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor regimen, it is recommended to start pitavastatin and, for patients on all other regimens, it is recommended to start atorvastatin at 10 mg daily. A lower dose is recommended because atorvastatin is partially metabolized by CYP3A. Pravastatin is not recommended any longer, because it is not as potent as the other two mentioned above. Now with the advent of antiretroviral regimens containing cobicistat, which is also an inhibitor of CYP 3A4, it is also contraindicated to initiate statins that are highly metabolized by CYP3A. While rosuvastatin is not metabolized by CYP3A4, five- to sevenfold increases in rosuvastatin levels are seen when co-administered with a boosted protease-inhibitor regimen or a regimen including cobicistat; therefore it is recommended to start rosuvastatin at a lower dose of 10 mg daily. Hepatitis B co-infection can be adequately treated with tenofovir alafenamide with no resistance seen in studies where patients are compliant. Therefore this patient should not be developing transaminitis due to viral hepatitis. A hepatitis D superinfection is possible, but unlikely. Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune disease of the small intralobular bile ducts that characteristically leads to drastic elevation in alkaline phosphatase levels, which was not seen in this case. However, there are biliary tract disorders that are more common among persons living with HIV , including acalculous cholecystitis and AIDS cholangiopathy. ACE-I are not known to cause hepatic impairment. In patients with renal impairment, decreased elimination of ACE-I can be seen leading to increased serum creatinine levels.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q35

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of increased abdominal weight gain and generalized muscle weakness. She had been found to have HIV 8 years previously when she was diagnosed in pregnancy. She was initially treated with zidovudine/lamivudine and lopinavir/ ritonavir during pregnancy and continued it until the previous year when she switched to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine/cobicistat/elvitegravir for ART simplification. She also had a history of seasonal allergies and a sporting injury to her right knee. In addition to ART , she was taking OTC antihistamines, intranasal fluticasone spray, and ibuprofen.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toxicity from nasal spray Cases of iatrogenic Cushing’s syndrome have been reported in patients who are co-administered antiretroviral boosting agents ritonavir or cobicistat with cytochrome 3A metabolized corticosteroids. This can include inhaled, intranasal, and intraarticular corticosteroids, which the patient may be acquiring over the counter or from other providers.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q38

questions.lead_in: The K103N mutation confers resistance to which of the following antiretroviral medications?
questions.explanation: Efavirenz K103N is the most common mutation associated with efavirenz resistance. This mutation also confers resistance to delavirdine and nevirapine, but not rilpivirine and etravirine.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q46

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman attended outpatient clinic having recently moved to the United States from Zimbabwe. She was not on antiretroviral therapy but reported receiving ART during delivery of her first child and antenatally during her second pregnancy. Investigations: CD4 count 370 cells/μL HIV viral load 36,000 copies/mL HIV genotype: Y181C mutation detected
questions.lead_in: What antiretroviral agent is contraindicated with this mutation?
questions.explanation: Nevirapine Y181C is selected in patients treated with nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors. It is the signature mutation for nevirapine and causes high-level reduction in nevirapine susceptibility, intermediate-level reduction in rilpivirine and etravirine susceptibility, and low-level reduction in efavirenz susceptibility.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q21

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man was admitted with a 6-week history of cough, fatigue, ∼10 lb weight loss, night sweats, and fever. He had recently been diagnosed with HIV . He had been born in Thailand but moved to the United States 10 years ago. He had been in prison for 2 years and was PPD negative at that time. Investigations: CD4 count 312/μL HIV VL 385, 000 copies /mL CXR: left upper lobe infiltrates Sputum microscopy: abundant acid-fast bacilli seen; Xpert MTB/RIF positive for both MTB and an rpo B gene mutation MDR-TB was suspected; it was thought that he would need between five and seven active antituberculosis drugs during the initiation phase.
questions.lead_in: What would be the best course of action?

options.text: Defer TB treatment for 2 weeks and start ART now
Start ART within 2 weeks and start TB treatment now
Start both TB and ART treatment now
Start TB treatment now and defer ART for 2–8 weeks
Start TB treatment now plus steroids and defer ART for 2–8 weeks

questions.explanation: Start TB treatment now and defer ART for 2–8 weeks Tuberculosis treatment should always be started once the clinician determines the diagnosis. In HIV-TB co-infection, ART should be initiated within 2 weeks only if CD4 count is <50/μL. In all other cases with CD4 count ≥50 initiation of ART should be started within 8 weeks, with exception of TB involving the CNS, where ART should be delayed for the first 8 weeks.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q17

questions.stem: A 48-year-old presented with extensive bruising on his left thigh after a minor injury 2 days earlier. Two weeks previously he had been started on rivaroxaban for a pulmonary thromboembolism and right lower extremity deep vein thrombosis. He was known to have well-controlled HIV , treated with elvitegravir/cobicistat/tenofovir/ emtricitabine.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his hematoma?
questions.explanation: Drug interaction This patient is suffering from a drug–drug interaction between his rivaroxaban and the cobicistat in his antiretroviral therapy. Cobicistat is an inhibitor of CYP 3A4 and would lead to higher plasma concentrations of the rivaroxaban, which could lead to hemorrhagic events. Therefore, it is not recommended to start rivaroxaban in patients on an ART regimen with cobicistat. Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) is considered an AIDS-defining illness and is typically seen in patients with advanced disease (CD4 cell count <100 cells/ μL). Primary CNS lymphoma and primary effusion lymphoma may also be seen in patients with advanced disease. The most common NHL seen in patients with HIV is B-cell lymphoma, followed by Burkett’s lymphoma. Plasmablastic lymphomas are rare but are also more common in people with HIV . The clinical presentation is also not characteristic, with no B-type symptoms, growing masses, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly. This patient does not have any other clinical features suggesting a thrombotic microangiopathy, thrombocytopenic purpura, or hemolytic uremic syndrome with signs of systemic organ dysfunction, which are all more common in patients infected with HIV . Protein C and S deficiencies are usually seen in patients with advanced disease and co-infection with an opportunistic infection. Protein C and S deficiency usually result in hypercoagulability manifesting as venous thromboembolism or arterial thrombosis. There have been case reports of patients developing warfarin-induced skin necrosis with protein C and S deficiency. Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder. Mild type 1 WBD may well manifest later in life when uncovered by antiplatelet medications; however, type 3 WBD usually presents in infancy or early childhood with bleeding provoked by minor trauma.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q19

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man attended for routine follow-up. He had HIV treated with tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine + twice-daily raltegravir. He had been diagnosed with a peptic ulcer and had started taking lansoprazole. His brother had recently died from a drug overdose, and the patient had been drinking alcohol heavily in response. As a result he was finding it difficult to remember to take his medication. Investigations: 2 Weeks Before Clinic Day of Clinic CD4 count / μL 395 HIV RNA copies/ml 2050 3950 HIV resistance assay Q148R mutation detected
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate antiretroviral regimen?

options.text: Tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine + atazanavir/ cobicistat once daily
Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine + ritonavir boosted darunavir once daily

questions.explanation: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine + ritonavir boosted darunavir once daily Q148R is a mutation that reduced susceptibility to both raltegravir and elvitegravir. Alone, there is evidence that Q148R confers low-level resistance to dolutegravir, and therefore if dolutegravir is used it should be dosed twice daily. Co-administration of atazanavir with a proton pump inhibitor is not recommended.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q20

questions.stem: A 48-year-old Senegalese man was found to have HIV on routine screening with a fourth-generation combined p24 Ag/Ab ELISA. A confirmatory test with a second-generation ELISA for IgG to differentiate between HIV-1 and HIV-2 infection detected HIV-2 antibodies. He was negative for HIV-1 antibodies and an HIV-1 RNA viral load was negative. An HIV-2 RNA viral load was sent to the reference laboratory. His CD4 count was 458 cells/μL (mm3).
questions.lead_in: What class of antiretrovirals is HIV-2 intrinsically resistant to?
questions.explanation: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors The NNRTI binding pocket is structurally different in HIV-2, conferring innate resistance onto this class of drugs. They should not be used in the treatment of HIV-2.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q47

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man attended the sexual health clinic following partner notification for gonorrhea. He was screened for rectal, urethral, and pharyngeal gonorrhea and chlamydia, and had epidemiologic treatment for gonorrhea with intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin. Given his high-risk sexual behavior (>30 partners in the preceding 3 months, unprotected insertive and receptive anal sex, participation in chemsex parties) he requested a point of care HIV test. This was positive, and a laboratory sample confirmed HIV and hepatitis C infection. CD4 count was 525 cells/μL, HIV viral load 12,458 copies/mL. Treatment was recommended given his co-infection status and as he wanted to reduce the risk of transmission to partners. A baseline HIV resistance screen was obtained prior to starting Atripla (tenofovir, emtricitabine, efavirenz).
questions.lead_in: What mutation in his resistance test would predict likely treatment failure with efavirenz?
questions.explanation: Y181C Amino acid substitutions such as K103N or Y181C prevent NNRTIs binding.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q48

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of fever, sore throat, and a rash. On examination she had a maculopapular rash and generalized lymphadenopathy. Investigations: Creatinine 0.7 mg/dL AST 65 units/L ALT 96 units/L Bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL EBV IgM positive, IgG positive, EBNA positive HIV Ab/Ag test negative HIV viral load 1.2 million copies/mL
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine +atazanavir/ cobicistat Initiation of ART in symptomatic acute HIV reduces symptoms and is now recommended. As a HLA B*5701 result is not available, abacavir-based regimens should be avoided. In the setting of acute infection, resistance assays may not be readily available, as in this case. In the absence of a resistance assay a protease-based or dolutegravir-based regimen is recommended pending results. Tenofovir alafenamide+cobicis tat+elvitegravir is incorrect as it is an incomplete regimen.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q21

questions.lead_in: Hypersensitivity to what drug can be predicted by HLAB*5701 testing?
questions.explanation: Abacavir Abacavir hypersensitivity can be predicted by testing for the HLAB*5701 allele. The syndrome can be life-threatening and can manifest with fever and other constitutional symptoms, rash, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, and dyspnea.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q44

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman attended for review after a positive pregnancy test. She was known to have HIV and was taking tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine/efavirenz. She reported ongoing compliance with her medication. She estimated that she was 7 weeks pregnant. Investigations: CD4 count 550 cells/μL HIV viral load undetectable
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Advise her to consider termination due to the risk of teratogenicity
Continue current ART and routine monitoring
Stop ART and recommence during the 2nd trimester
Switch to ritonavir-boosted darunavir, zidovudine, and emtricitabine

questions.explanation: Continue current ART and routine monitoring HIV-infected pregnant women established on ART who present for care during the 1st trimester should continue treatment during pregnancy, provided the regimen is tolerated and effective in suppressing viral replication. Women who become pregnant on efavirenz-containing regimens who are virally suppressed and tolerating it should continue their current regimens. In the past efavirenz was linked with teratogenicity based on animal studies; however, increased teratogenicity has not been seen in the babies of mothers exposed to efavirenz in the 1st trimester in registry studies and meta-analyses. Therefore guidelines recommend continuing treatment: http://aidsinfo.nih.gov/contentfiles/lvgu idelines/PerinatalGL.pd. There is no data on cobicistat in pregnancy, therefore for present protease inhibitors should be ritonavir-boosted.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q34

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman was reviewed with a new diagnosis of HIV and hepatitis B co-infection. A pregnancy test was negative. Despite multiple educational meetings she declined HIV treatment but was interested in hepatitis B treatment. Investigations: AST 89 IU/L ALT 98 units/L CD4 count 434 cells/μL HIV viral load 55,000 copies/mL HBsAg positive HBV viral load 540,000 IU/mL Liver biopsy showed significant fibrosis but no cirrhosis
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to offer?
questions.explanation: Peginterferon alfa 2B The patient is refusing HIV treatment at this time. The concern is that using an agent for her hepatitis that also has activity against HIV would lead to the development of HIV resistance. Entecavir, lamivudine, tenofovir, and emtricitabine are all active against both HIV and HBV . Only peginterferon alfa 2B alone will not lead to HIV-resistance. Remember that interferon therapy has many disadvantages, multiple side effects (i.e., influenza-like syndrome, myalgias, depression, fatigue, etc.) and is only given IM. If the patient would have accepted treatment for both HIV and HBV , then combination therapy with tenofovir, emtricitabine, and dolutegravir would have been the optimal choice. This regimen offers three active drugs against HIV as recommended by the DHHS guidelines and at the same time would offer two active drugs against hepatitis B (tenofovir and emtricitabine).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q8

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman from Zimbabwe presented with a 2-week history of increasing confusion, ataxia, headache, and fevers. She was admitted and a lumbar puncture performed after a CT scan of her head. Investigations: HIV-1 Ag/Ab positive CD4 5 cells/μL HIV viral load 225 000 copies/mL Serum CRAG positive CSF: opening pressure 450 mmH2O (120–250) Protein 0.9 g/L (0.15–0.45) Glucose 2.3 mmol/L (plasma glucose 7.2) White blood cells 0.05 ×109/L(50/mm3), 90% lymphocytes Cryptococcal antigen positive CSF cultures: growth on Sab plates consistent with Cryptococcus neoformans She was started on liposomal amphotericin B and 5-flucytosine.
questions.lead_in: When should she be started on antiretrovirals?

options.text: When a repeat CSF is culture negative
When her serum CRAG becomes negative

questions.explanation: After 4 weeks of antifungals Cryptococcosis is one of the few opportunistic infections for which early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (less than 2 weeks) is associated with increased mortality. It is generally recommended to delay ART initiation to at least 4 weeks after start of antifungal therapy to avoid severe immune reconstitution syndrome.

questions.question: Antiretroviral drug interactions with proton pump inhibitors.

parts.text: Name two antiretroviral therapies that interact with proton pump inhibitors.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 antiretroviral therapies that interact with PPI's.

questions.model_answer: (1) Rilpivirine - absorption is gastric pH dependent; PPIs should not be coadministered. (2) Atazanavir (boosted or unboosted) - absorption requires a low gastric pH, so PPIs markedly reduce exposure.

cohort_answer.text: RPV, ATV/r

questions.question: Integrase inhibitor metabolism by cytochrome P-450 3A4.

parts.text: Name one integrase inhibitor that interacts with CYP3A4.

parts_raw.text: Name 1 integrase inhibitor that interacts with CYP 3A4.

questions.model_answer: Elvitegravir - a CYP3A4 substrate, which is why it is coformulated with the CYP3A inhibitor cobicistat; the resulting fixed-dose products alter levels of CYP3A and CYP2D6 substrates. (Dolutegravir and bictegravir are also partly CYP3A4 metabolized but neither induces nor inhibits it.)

cohort_answer.text: EVG/c

questions.question: Pharmacokinetic boosting agents used in antiretroviral therapy.

parts.text: Name two medications that can be used as boosters.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 medications that be used as boosters.

questions.model_answer: (1) Ritonavir - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor used at subtherapeutic dose to boost protease inhibitors. (2) Cobicistat - CYP3A inhibitor with no antiviral activity, used to boost elvitegravir, atazanavir and darunavir.

cohort_answer.text: Ritonavir, cobicistat

questions.question: Antiretroviral toxicity compounded by long-term NSAID use.

parts.text: Name one antiretroviral therapy that can cause complications with long-term exposure to NSAIDs.

parts_raw.text: Name 1 antiretroviral therapy that can cause complications with long term exposure to NSAIDs.

questions.model_answer: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate - cumulative nephrotoxicity (declining GFR, proximal tubulopathy) that is additive with chronic NSAID use; monitor creatinine, urinalysis and urine electrolytes.

cohort_answer.text: TDF

questions.question: An HIV-positive female is stable and has been managed on tenofovir, emtricitabine and efavirenz.
questions.question_raw: A HIV positive female is stable and has been managed on tenofovir, emtricitabine and efavirenz.

parts.text: She becomes pregnant. What would you suggest for antiretroviral therapy during pregnancy?
In another scenario, the patient is now HIV positive but treatment naive. What would you treat with?

parts_raw.text: She becomes pregnant. What would you suggest for antiretroviral therapy during pregnancy?
In another scenario, the patient is now HIV positive but treatment naïve. What would you treat with?

questions.model_answer:
a) Continue the same tenofovir/emtricitabine/efavirenz regimen. She is virologically suppressed, and efavirenz may be continued in a person who presents for care during the first trimester; a definitive association between efavirenz and human birth defects was not confirmed in meta-analysis, and the risk of losing suppression by switching outweighs any theoretical teratogenic benefit. Confirm suppression with a viral load and continue through delivery.
b) A dual-NRTI backbone plus an integrase inhibitor: dolutegravir + tenofovir (TDF or TAF)/emtricitabine, bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine, or raltegravir + tenofovir/emtricitabine. In a woman of child-bearing potential do a pregnancy test before starting dolutegravir because of the possible neural tube defect signal with first-trimester exposure; raltegravir-based therapy is a reasonable alternative.

cohort_answer.text: Continue with current regimen. || DRV/r or RAL /TDF/FTC.

questions.question: Give one reason or clinical scenario for which you would NOT recommend each of the following HIV drugs in a first-line regimen.
questions.question_raw: Give 1 reason/clinical scenario for which you would NOT recommend the following HIV drugs in a 1st line regimen

parts.text: Abacavir (NRTI)
Efavirenz (NNRTI)
Atazanavir (PI)
Tenofovir (NRTI)
Elvitegravir-cobicistat (boosted INSTI)
Rilpivirine (NNRTI)

parts_raw.text: Abacavir (NRTI)
Efavirenz (NNRTI)
Atazanavir (PI)
Tenofovir (NRTI)
Elvitegravir-cobicistat (boosted INSTI)
Rilipivirine (NNRTI)

questions.model_answer:
a) Abacavir: patient is HLA-B*5701 positive - risk of fatal hypersensitivity syndrome; also avoid in a patient with established cardiovascular disease or a baseline viral load >100,000 copies/mL.
b) Efavirenz: preexisting psychiatric disease (depression, suicidality) given its CNS toxicity; also a person of child-bearing potential not on effective contraception.
c) Atazanavir: a patient requiring a proton pump inhibitor, since atazanavir absorption needs a low gastric pH; also avoid in severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic insufficiency.
d) Tenofovir (TDF): preexisting renal insufficiency or osteopenia/osteoporosis - cumulative nephrotoxicity and bone mineral density loss.
e) Elvitegravir-cobicistat: renal impairment - the TDF-containing coformulation must not be started with a creatinine clearance <70 mL/min (and stopped below 50), the TAF version not below 30 mL/min; also numerous CYP3A/2D6 interactions (contraindicated with lovastatin, simvastatin, rifampin).
f) Rilpivirine: pretreatment viral load >100,000 copies/mL (or CD4 <200 cells/mm3) - higher rates of virologic failure and resistance; also a patient on a PPI.

cohort_answer.text: Abacavir: HLA B5701+ (hypersensitivity reaction). Efavirenz: Psychiatric conditions; Pregnant/planning pregnancy (neural tube defect association in non-human primates). Atazanavir: Co-infected with TB requiring TB treatment (PI-Rifamycin interactions); Patient on PPI; Kidney stones; Diabetes. Tenofovir: Renal dysfunction; Bone density issues. Elvitegravir-cobicistat: Renal dysfunction (CrCl<70), elevated TG; No data in pregnancy. Rilpivirine: High viral load >100,000 copies/ml & CD4<200 (virologic failure).

parts.text: Give three first-line regimens recommended by guidelines.
In general, what are the indications to start antiretroviral therapy?

parts_raw.text: Give three first-line regimens recommended by guidelines
In general, what are the indications to start antiretroviral therapy?

questions.model_answer:
a) All must avoid abacavir (HLA-B*5701 positive, and inferior at viral load >100,000) and avoid NNRTIs (K103N): (1) Dolutegravir + tenofovir (TDF or TAF)/emtricitabine. (2) Bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine. (3) Raltegravir + tenofovir (TDF or TAF)/emtricitabine.
b) Antiretroviral therapy is recommended for all people with HIV regardless of CD4 count. Conditions favouring especially early/urgent initiation: acute or recent HIV infection; AIDS-defining conditions including HIV-associated dementia and AIDS-associated malignancy; pregnancy; HIV-associated nephropathy; CD4 <200 cells/mm3; acute opportunistic infection; HIV RNA >100,000 copies/mL; CD4 decline >100 cells/mm3/yr; hepatitis B or hepatitis C coinfection. Treatment as prevention in serodiscordant couples is an additional indication (96% transmission reduction in HPTN 052). Patient readiness and adherence must be addressed before starting.

cohort_answer.text:
K103N and Y181C mutations confer resistance to Efavirenz and Nevirapine. M184V mutation – decreases susceptibility to FTC / 3TC but increases susceptibility to TDF, usually first mutation to appear
Indications to start ART: All HIV positive individuals regardless of CD4 count. START and TEMPRANO trials were associated with decreased mortality when ARVs were started when CD4 counts >500. Delayed ART: crypto (2-10 weeks after starting tx), TB (CD4>50, start within 8 weeks)

questions.question: An HIV patient has a CD4 count of 550 cells/mm3.
questions.question_raw: HIV with CD4 of 550.

parts.text: Please provide four benefits to starting HIV therapy.
The HLA test is pending; name two potential regimens to start the patient on.
Four indications for resistance testing.

parts_raw.text: Please provide 4 benefits to start HIV therapy.
HLA test is pending, name two potential regimens to start the patient on.
Four indications for resistance setting.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Reduced HIV-related morbidity and mortality - risk of AIDS and death rises continuously across all CD4 strata, so treating at any count lowers it. (2) Reduced non-AIDS morbidity and mortality (cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, malignancy) attributable to ongoing viraemia and inflammation. (3) Preservation and reconstitution of CD4 counts - patients starting above 350 cells/mm3 usually normalize their counts, whereas those starting below 200 largely do not. (4) Prevention of onward transmission - 96% reduction in HIV transmission to serodiscordant partners with early ART (HPTN 052), plus reduced extrapulmonary tuberculosis.
b) Two abacavir-free regimens (HLA-B*5701 result pending): (1) Dolutegravir + tenofovir (TDF or TAF)/emtricitabine. (2) Bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine (raltegravir + tenofovir/emtricitabine is an acceptable alternative).
c) (1) At the time of HIV diagnosis/entry into care. (2) Before initiating antiretroviral therapy (baseline genotype of reverse transcriptase and protease). (3) In pregnant persons before starting therapy. (4) At virologic failure of a regimen with HIV RNA >1000 copies/mL - performed, if possible, while the patient is still on the failing regimen. Add tropism testing if a CCR5 antagonist is contemplated.

parts.text: Name the trial supporting initiation of antiretrovirals with a CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm3.

parts_raw.text: HIV with CD4 of 550, name trial supporting initiation of ARVs with CD4 >500.

questions.model_answer: The START trial (Strategic Timing of Antiretroviral Treatment), which randomized ART-naive adults with CD4 >500 cells/mm3 to immediate versus deferred therapy and showed a significant reduction in serious AIDS and non-AIDS events with immediate treatment. TEMPRANO (Cote d'Ivoire) gave concordant results, and HPTN 052 showed benefit plus a 96% reduction in transmission at a median CD4 of about 450.

questions.model_answer:
a) Cobicistat (the pharmacologic booster in the elvitegravir single-tablet regimen) is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor and is contraindicated with simvastatin and lovastatin - markedly raised statin levels cause myopathy/rhabdomyolysis. A hypertensive diabetic is very likely to be on a statin.

b) Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF).

c) A TAF-based single tablet: bictegravir/emtricitabine/TAF, or elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/TAF. Both are acceptable at CrCl >=30 mL/min and TAF has less renal and bone toxicity; the TDF-containing elvitegravir tablet must be stopped once CrCl falls below 50 mL/min.

d) Zidovudine - bone marrow suppression (anemia, neutropenia). Atazanavir - indirect hyperbilirubinemia/jaundice. Efavirenz - CNS adverse effects (vivid dreams, insomnia, dizziness, poor concentration; also teratogenicity/neural tube defects). Nevirapine - hepatotoxicity and severe rash (more frequent than with efavirenz). Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate - nephrotoxicity/proximal tubulopathy with declining GFR (and reduced bone mineral density). Abacavir - HLA-B*5701-linked hypersensitivity reaction (fever, abdominal pain, rash within 2 weeks), which can be fatal.
questions.beyond_mandell: Zidovudine marrow suppression and the dolutegravir/bictegravir-metformin interaction (raised metformin levels; HHS guidelines advise limiting metformin to 1000 mg/day) are not in this chapter slice.

cohort_answer.text: Drug interaction: Cobicistat is a CYP3A4 inhibitor and may significantly increase levels of some statins (simvastatin, lovastatin) - coadministration contraindicated; Dolutegravir and bictegravir may significantly increase adverse effects of metformin. Offending drug: TDF (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate). Switch to: EVG/cobi/TAF/FTC (Genvoya) or Biktarvy

parts.text: What is the preferred management of HIV during pregnancy (regimens) and peripartum?

questions.model_answer:
a) Antepartum: start or continue ART in every pregnant person, at any gestational age and any CD4 count, aiming for HIV RNA <50 copies/mL by delivery; obtain a genotype before starting but do not delay therapy. Preferred regimens are a dual-NRTI backbone (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine, or abacavir/lamivudine if HLA-B*5701 negative) plus dolutegravir 50 mg daily; alternatives are raltegravir 400 mg twice daily or ritonavir-boosted darunavir twice daily. Efavirenz is avoided around conception because of neural tube defects; boosted protease inhibitors carry a possible preterm delivery signal. Monitor viral load monthly until suppressed, then at least every trimester and at 34-36 weeks.

Intrapartum: continue oral ART. Give intravenous zidovudine, 2 mg/kg over 1 hour then 1 mg/kg/h until the cord is clamped, if HIV RNA is >1000 copies/mL or unknown near delivery; it is not required if HIV RNA is <=50 copies/mL on ART with good adherence, and may be considered for 50-999 copies/mL. Schedule cesarean delivery at 38 weeks for HIV RNA >1000 copies/mL near delivery; vaginal delivery is appropriate if suppressed. Avoid invasive fetal monitoring and artificial rupture of membranes when viraemic.

Postpartum: continue maternal ART for life, start infant zidovudine prophylaxis (or presumptive three-drug therapy if maternal viraemia), infant HIV NAAT testing, and formula feeding in Canada.
questions.beyond_mandell: Perinatal specifics are from the HHS Perinatal HIV guidelines; the chapter provides only ART pharmacology, IV zidovudine dosing and the dolutegravir/efavirenz pregnancy safety data.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answer avoids dolutegravir in the first trimester and prefers raltegravir or a boosted PI; that reflects the interim 2018 signal described in the chapter, but subsequent Tsepamo data did not confirm the neural tube defect risk and dolutegravir is now preferred throughout pregnancy.

cohort_answer.text: 2 NRTI backbones (ABC/3TC or TDF/FTC or TDF/3TC) + RAL (don't use DTG in 1st trimester) or ATV/r or DRV/r. Intravenous (IV) zidovudine: if HIV RNA is known or suspected to be >1,000 copies/mL (or if HIV RNA is unknown) near delivery; not required for women receiving ART with HIV RNA ≤50 copies/mL during late pregnancy/near delivery and no adherence concerns; may be considered for women with HIV RNA between 50 and 999. Scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks' gestation (compared to 39 weeks for most indications) for women who have HIV RNA >1,000 copies/mL near delivery

questions.model_answer:
a) Treat now. Overwhelming data support universal ART for all people with HIV regardless of CD4 count; the goal of therapy is plasma HIV RNA <50 copies/mL, and same-day/rapid initiation after diagnosis is feasible and beneficial.
b) (1) Personal benefit: immediate ART reduces HIV-related morbidity and mortality and raises CD4 counts across all CD4 strata, with reduced rates of extrapulmonary tuberculosis in HPTN 052. (2) Public health benefit: treatment as prevention, with a 96% reduction in transmission to a serodiscordant partner in HPTN 052 (92% in an observational cohort of ~3400 serodiscordant couples).
c) (1) The patient is not ready or willing to commit to lifelong therapy: adherence is critical, and deferral until adherence can be maximized is preferable to suboptimal or incomplete therapy. (2) The burden and toxicity of the regimen (drug adverse effects, interactions, pill burden, comorbidities) outweigh the anticipated benefit in that individual.

cohort_answer.text: Guidelines: Treat now. Reasons to treat: Reduction in risk of propagation to others; Reduction of propagation to sanctuary sites (progression to AIDS). Reasons not to: TB meningitis/crypto meningitis; Not willing to start therapy.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Abacavir: HLA-B*5701-positive patient (risk of fatal hypersensitivity); also avoid with pre-existing cardiac risk factors, and use with caution if viral load >100,000 copies/mL (ACTG 5202). (2) Efavirenz: pre-existing psychiatric illness, given CNS toxicity in up to 50% and a possible association with suicidality; also avoid in a person of child-bearing potential not using effective contraception. (3) Atazanavir: patient requiring a proton pump inhibitor or unable to take it with food (absorption needs a low gastric pH), or Gilbert syndrome/hyperbilirubinemia leading to discontinuation. (4) Tenofovir (TDF): chronic kidney disease or low bone mineral density, given progressive GFR decline and bone loss with TDF (TAF is not recommended if creatinine clearance <30 mL/min). (5) Elvitegravir-cobicistat: renal impairment (TDF coformulation not to be used if creatinine clearance <70 mL/min, stop below 50; TAF coformulation not below 30) or polypharmacy/rifampin, lovastatin, simvastatin because of cobicistat CYP3A and CYP2D6 interactions; also requires food. (6) Rilpivirine: baseline viral load >100,000 copies/mL or CD4 <200 cells/mm3 (higher virologic failure and resistance), or need for a proton pump inhibitor. (7) Lopinavir/ritonavir: dyslipidemia or cardiovascular risk, plus a high pill burden and twice-daily dosing; it has been shown non-superior to better-tolerated boosted PIs. (8) Nevirapine: risk of rash and hepatotoxicity, which are more frequent than with efavirenz; also early virologic failure when combined with a tenofovir prodrug plus emtricitabine/lamivudine.

cohort_answer.text: Abacavir = HLAB5701+, heart disease. Efavirenz = Psychiatric illness/CNS side effects. Atazanavir = Poor food safety (needs co-administration with food), Gilbert's (increases bilirubin), low bone mineral density. Tenofovir = Avoid if CKD (GFR <50), osteoporosis, TAF if GFR <30. Elvitegravir-cobicistat = Should be taken with food, poor food safety, lots of drug interactions - avoid if polypharmacy, renal failure. Rilpivirine = VL >100,000, CD4 <200 (higher virologic failure), fatigue, rash. Lopinavir/ritonavir = Heart disease, dyslipidemia. Nevirapine = Increases cholesterol (avoid in dyslipidemia), hepatotoxicity and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Summary: Dyslipidemia/heart disease - Abacavir, nevirapine, lopinavir/ritonavir; High viral load - Abacavir and rilpivirine; Renal failure - TDF and TAF; Psychiatric illness - Efavirenz.

questions.model_answer:
a) TAF is a prodrug of tenofovir, a nucleotide adenosine 5'-monophosphate derivative. After ingestion it is hydrolyzed to tenofovir, then phosphorylated and incorporated into HIV DNA, causing chain termination; it has low affinity for cellular DNA polymerases including mitochondrial pol-gamma, and is also active against hepatitis B.
b) TAF delivers tenofovir more efficiently into cells: it produces higher intracellular tenofovir concentrations and lower plasma concentrations than TDF, so a 25 mg dose (10 mg when boosted with cobicistat) is virologically non-inferior to 300 mg of TDF.
c) (1) Nephrotoxicity - smaller serum creatinine increases and less proteinuria. (2) Bone mineral density loss - less decline at hip and spine, with improvement on switching from TDF. (Note the trade-off: fasting lipid levels rise with TAF relative to TDF.)

cohort_answer.text: MOA: a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI), analog of adenosine 5'-monophosphate, interferes with HIV viral RNA-dependent DNA polymerase inhibiting viral replication. Lower dose: as an alanine ester prodrug converted intracellularly by hydrolysis to tenofovir then phosphorylated to active tenofovir diphosphate, lower doses can be used. Less common side effects: bone mineral density loss/osteoporosis, kidney injury.

Rilpivirine - NNRTI, inhibits HIV-encoded reverse transcriptase enzyme in the host cell cytoplasm, blocking conversion of single-stranded viral RNA to double-stranded DNA and preventing incorporation of HIV genetic material into host DNA. Difference: NNRTI binds to reverse transcriptase adjacent to the active site, causing structural changes preventing addition of nucleosides to the growing DNA chain.
3 criteria before starting: Be virologically suppressed; on stable oral regimen for 6-12 months; no documented resistance mutations to Cabotegravir or Rilpivirine; be willing/able to adhere to clinic visits for IM injections; Hepatitis B negative.

parts_raw.text: What is the mechanism of action of TAF?
What is the reason that TAF can be given at a lower dose than tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)?
What are the two side effects of TDF that are reduced in TAF?

questions.model_answer:
a) TAF is a prodrug of tenofovir, a nucleotide (adenosine 5'-monophosphate) analogue. After ingestion it is hydrolyzed to tenofovir, then phosphorylated intracellularly to tenofovir diphosphate, which is incorporated into viral DNA by reverse transcriptase and causes chain termination; it has low affinity for cellular DNA polymerases including mitochondrial pol-gamma.
b) TAF is more stable in plasma and delivers drug intracellularly, producing higher intracellular tenofovir diphosphate concentrations with much lower plasma tenofovir concentrations than TDF, so an equivalent antiviral effect is achieved at a much lower dose (25 mg vs 300 mg).
c) (1) Nephrotoxicity/decline in renal function (smaller creatinine rise, less proteinuria). (2) Decreased bone mineral density.

questions.model_answer: a) Dolutegravir plus lamivudine (dolutegravir/lamivudine single-tablet regimen), provided he is HBsAg-negative and has no baseline resistance. Rationale from the drug properties: every tenofovir- and TAF-containing single-tablet regimen is excluded (TAF is not recommended below CrCl 30 mL/min, TDF requires dose reduction in renal insufficiency and is nephrotoxic); the elvitegravir/cobicistat co-formulations are excluded (TDF-based not to be used below CrCl 70 and stopped below 50; TAF-based not below CrCl 30); bictegravir/emtricitabine/TAF is excluded (not to be used below CrCl 30). Dolutegravir needs no renal dose adjustment, is glucuronidated, and its rise in serum creatinine reflects blocked tubular secretion, not a fall in GFR. Note the lamivudine component still needs renal dose adjustment at this CrCl, so many would give dolutegravir plus dose-adjusted lamivudine as separate tablets; alternatives that are not single-tablet regimens include darunavir/ritonavir plus raltegravir or darunavir/ritonavir plus lamivudine. Dolutegravir also raises metformin levels (OCT2 inhibition), so metformin must be dose-limited or stopped — and metformin is in any case contraindicated at CrCl 20.

parts.text: Recognition and management, especially the choice of future antiretroviral therapy

parts_raw.text: Recognition and management (esp choice of future ART)

questions.model_answer: a) Recognition: type B lactic acidosis from NRTI inhibition of mitochondrial DNA polymerase-gamma, classically with stavudine, zidovudine and didanosine; insidious GI prodrome (nausea, abdominal pain), weight loss, fatigue, then tachycardia, tachypnea, hepatomegaly/steatosis with transaminitis, and in severe cases pancreatitis, organ failure and death (mortality high with lactate >10 mmol/L); women and obese patients at higher risk. Confirm with elevated lactate, anion-gap metabolic acidosis and no hypoperfusion. Management: stop all NRTIs immediately, supportive care (IV fluids, avoid metformin/other mitochondrial toxins, thiamine/riboflavin/L-carnitine have been used), monitor lactate to resolution. Future ART: never resume the offending agent; rebuild with drugs of low mitochondrial toxicity — abacavir, lamivudine/emtricitabine, or a tenofovir prodrug (tenofovir has low affinity for mtDNA pol-gamma), or use an NRTI-sparing/2-drug regimen with an INSTI plus a boosted PI.

questions.question: Discuss HIV resistance testing.
questions.question_raw: HIV resistance testing

parts.text: Define phenotypic versus genotypic testing

parts_raw.text: Define phenotypic vs genotypic?

questions.model_answer: a) Genotypic assays sequence HIV genes (reverse transcriptase, protease, and integrase when indicated) from patient isolates and report mutations that confer resistance; they are cheaper, faster, and generally preferred, particularly in antiretroviral-naive patients. Phenotypic assays use cultured patient isolates and report fold change in drug susceptibility in the presence of drug; they are more expensive but useful for interpreting complex resistance patterns (e.g. multiple PI mutations). Virtual phenotypes predict phenotype from genotype using a matched library. Both require plasma HIV RNA above roughly 500-1000 copies/mL, and testing should be done while the patient is still on the failing regimen.

cohort_answer.text: Genotypic test detects drug resistance mutations in relevant genes. Requires VL>500-1000. TAT 1-2 weeks. Increased sensitivity over phenotypic for detecting wild type and resistance. Reduced costs. Preferred. Phenotypic testing: measures ability of virus to grow in different concentrations of ARV drug. TAT 2-3 weeks. More expensive than genotypic

parts.text: What factors might result in increased viral load?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Poor adherence, including temporary lapses that produce transient blips of 50-1000 copies/mL. (2) Inadequate drug exposure — drug-drug or drug-food interactions (e.g. rifampin, antacids, proton pump inhibitors), poor absorption, wrong dosing, intolerance. (3) Transmitted or emergent drug resistance to one or more regimen components. Distinguish a blip from true virologic failure — persistently detectable virus after prior suppression, or failure to suppress by 24 to 48 weeks — which should prompt resistance testing when HIV RNA is greater than 1000 copies/mL.

cohort_answer.text: Drug: Poor adherence; Suboptimal dosing due to drug-drug interactions, drug-food interactions, drug tolerability; Poor absorption. Virus: Prior or current resistance mutation; Acquisition of a new resistant virus. Virologic failure: inability to maintain suppression of viral replication to a new HIV RNA level <200

questions.model_answer: a) Do not change the regimen yet. A decline of at least 1 log10 by 4 weeks is expected, with suppression to less than 50 copies/mL by 16 to 24 weeks, so if the viral load is falling appropriately continue the same regimen and repeat HIV RNA every 4 to 8 weeks. Only if the viral load plateaus or rebounds, or fails to suppress by 4 to 6 months, obtain genotypic resistance testing (HIV RNA >1000 copies/mL) and construct a new regimen with at least two, preferably three, fully active drugs.

parts_raw.text: a) Class and MOA

questions.model_answer:
a) Entry inhibitor — CCR5 antagonist. It binds allosterically to the host CCR5 coreceptor and changes its conformation so gp120 cannot engage it, blocking viral entry/fusion; it is host-directed, not virus-directed.
b) Hepatotoxicity (including reported hypersensitivity-associated hepatitis, boxed warning), postural hypotension/dizziness, upper respiratory infections and cough, fever, rash, abdominal pain, diarrhea, musculoskeletal symptoms.
c) Maraviroc is cleared by hepatic CYP3A metabolism, so dose must be adjusted for interacting drugs: strong CYP3A inhibitors (ritonavir- or cobicistat-boosted PIs, azoles, clarithromycin) raise levels and require dose reduction to 150 mg twice daily; CYP3A inducers (efavirenz, etravirine, rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) lower levels and require 600 mg twice daily. Standard dose is 300 mg twice daily.
d) Treatment of HIV-1 infection (treatment-experienced, and licensed for naive patients) only when a coreceptor tropism assay shows exclusively CCR5-tropic virus; it is ineffective against CXCR4-using or dual/mixed-tropic virus, so tropism testing is mandatory before use and when a maraviroc-containing regimen fails.
questions.beyond_mandell: Maraviroc adverse-effect list and the CYP3A dose-adjustment bands (150/300/600 mg bid) come from the product monograph and DHHS ART guidelines; the narrative maraviroc section falls outside the pages supplied.

cohort_answer.text: a) Entry/CCR5 inhibitor; inhibits binding of HIV gp120 to CCR5 co-receptor by binding CCR5 and changing conformation. b) Common: postural hypotension, anaemia, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating, loss of appetite, flatulence, weakness, depression, insomnia, raised liver enzymes, rash. Rare: hepatitis, hypersensitivity reaction. c) Substrate of CYP3A: CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole/itraconazole, clarithromycin, lopinavir/ritonavir, atazanavir) increase exposure; CYP3A4 inducers (efavirenz, rifampicin, phenytoin, phenobarbital) reduce exposure; cotrimoxazole decreases renal clearance. d) Treatment experienced/naive patients with CCR5 tropism; not first line/switch medication in practice, used in resistance setting; may select CXCR4 tropic variants in heterotropic population (more rapid progression); all patients screened for viral co-receptor usage before starting, avoid if CXCR4-using virus present.

questions.model_answer:
(1) Start maternal combination antiretroviral therapy as soon as possible — pregnancy is an explicit indication for immediate ART, and full viral suppression is the single most effective intervention; if she declines ongoing therapy, at minimum intrapartum intravenous zidovudine.

(3) Infant antiretroviral prophylaxis started within 6 hours of birth (zidovudine alone for low-risk, or presumptive multidrug therapy such as zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine/raltegravir when the mother is untreated), plus complete avoidance of breastfeeding where replacement feeding is safe.

questions.question: Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF).

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action?
Why can it be used at a lower dose than tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)?

parts_raw.text: What is the mechanism of action
Why can use at lower dose than TDF

questions.model_answer:
a) Nucleotide reverse-transcriptase inhibitor prodrug. After ingestion TAF is hydrolyzed to tenofovir, then phosphorylated intracellularly to tenofovir diphosphate, which is incorporated into HIV DNA by reverse transcriptase and causes chain termination. Tenofovir has low affinity for cellular DNA polymerases including mitochondrial pol-γ, and is active against both HIV and HBV.
b) TAF is a more stable prodrug that delivers drug intracellularly — it produces higher intracellular tenofovir concentrations and lower plasma tenofovir concentrations than TDF, so a much smaller dose (25 mg, or 10 mg when boosted) achieves equivalent antiviral activity with less systemic exposure.
c) Less bone toxicity (smaller declines in bone mineral density) and less renal toxicity than TDF; the trade-off is that TDF gives lower lipid levels.

cohort_answer.text: MOA: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor - prevents HIV from replicating by competitively inhibiting reverse transcriptase enzyme and preventing DNA production (NNRTI works similarly but via noncompetitive inhibition). Lower dose reason: TAF is a prodrug absorbed more quickly than TDF and produces higher levels of active drug intracellularly, allowing smaller doses and less systemic exposure in blood and organs (bones and kidney where major adverse effects of tenofovir occur). Better side effects: Lower risk of decreased bone mineral density and nephrotoxicity

questions.model_answer:
a) Start ART within the first 2 weeks of beginning PCP treatment. Longer delay is associated with additional opportunistic infections and decreased survival; the exact day within that window depends on severity, ability to absorb oral drugs, and drug interactions. (PCP is not one of the exceptions - cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis is deferred 2-10 weeks; cryptosporidiosis and JC virus encephalitis are started as soon as feasible.) Caution: ART may worsen pulmonary function through IRIS as the recovering inflammatory response meets residual Pneumocystis antigen.
b) (1) Screening test for latent tuberculosis (TST or IGRA). (2) Toxoplasma gondii IgG serology (determines need for toxoplasmosis prophylaxis at CD4 <100). (3) Hepatitis B serology - anti-HBs/anti-HBc to define immunity and vaccination need (already immune here). (4) Hepatitis A serology to identify HAV-susceptible patients needing vaccination. (5) Coccidioides IgM/IgG serology if she lives in an endemic area (prophylaxis if positive and CD4 <250). (6) VZV serology/history of varicella or zoster to determine vaccine or post-exposure candidacy. Also: syphilis serology, and CD4 count/viral load monitoring to guide starting and stopping prophylaxis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Serum cryptococcal antigen screening at CD4 <100 and G6PD testing before dapsone are standard DHHS/IDSA OI-guideline additions not specified in this chapter text.

cohort_answer.text:

In an RCT of 282 patients with OIs other than TB, 63% of whom had definite or presumptive PCP, a significantly lower incidence of AIDS progression or death (a secondary study endpoint) was seen in subjects randomized to early (median 12 days after initiation of therapy for OI) versus deferred initiation of ART (median 45 days). Of note, no patients with PCP and respiratory failure requiring intubation were enrolled in the study, and initiating ART in such patients is problematic due to the lack of parenteral preparations and unpredictble absorption of oral medications, as well as potential drug interactions with agents commonly used in the ICU

questions.model_answer:
a) An exaggerated inflammatory response occurring after ART-induced immune reconstitution, directed at residual organisms or antigen of an opportunistic pathogen. Paradoxical IRIS worsens a recognized infection (e.g., raised ICP in cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis, worsening pulmonary function after PCP); unmasking IRIS reveals a subclinical infection such as CMV retinitis or MAC lymphadenitis. Ranges from mild and self-limiting to life-threatening and mimics both new opportunistic infection and treatment failure.
b) (1) Very low CD4 count with high viral load and a large untreated/subclinical opportunistic-infection burden, particularly CNS cryptococcal or tuberculous disease. (2) Early ART initiation relative to opportunistic-infection therapy, with rapid virologic suppression and CD4 recovery.
c) (1) Cryptococcus neoformans. (2) Toxoplasma gondii. (3) Mycobacterium tuberculosis. (4) JC virus (PML). Cytomegalovirus is an additional consideration.
d) Continue ART and pathogen-directed therapy. NSAIDs for non-severe IRIS. For severe or CNS IRIS, corticosteroids - e.g., prednisone 1.5 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks then 0.75 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks with taper over at least 4 weeks (TB-IRIS regimen); corticosteroids are indicated in cryptococcal disease specifically for management of IRIS. Control raised ICP with repeated lumbar punctures or CSF shunting (corticosteroids and mannitol do not reduce ICP). Immunosuppressive biologic agents for refractory life-threatening IRIS.

cohort_answer.text: IRIS description: An exaggerated inflammatory reaction to a disease-causing organism that may occur during immune reconstitution (recovery) following initiation of ARVs. Two forms occur: 'unmasking' IRIS where new symptoms of an undiagnosed infection appear, and 'paradoxical' IRIS, where a previously treated infection worsens after ARV therapy is started (https://clinicalinfo.hiv.gov/en/glossary/immune-reconstitution-inflammatory-syndrome-iris). Risk factors: Low CD4 count (<100); High Viral Load (early initiation of ARV before treatment of infection). Pathogens: Cryptococcus neoformans; JCV (PML-IRIS); Mycobacterium Tuberculosis; Toxoplasma; MAC; CMV (immune recovery uveitis). Treatment: 0.5-1mg/kg/day Prednisone equivalent as Dexamethasone, tapered over 2-6 weeks depending on clinical improvement (IDSA Cryptococcus 2010)

First confirm adherence, drug interactions and HBV/HIV resistance, and exclude other causes of the transaminitis (drug hepatotoxicity, HCV, HDV, alcohol). For the dyslipidemia, choose TAF-based or, if lipids dominate, TDF-based dosing (TDF is associated with lower lipids, TAF with less renal/bone toxicity) and avoid a boosted PI, which commonly causes dyslipidemia and insulin resistance — use an integrase inhibitor (dolutegravir or bictegravir) as the third agent; avoid abacavir given cardiovascular concerns and its lack of anti-HBV activity. parts.text: Two strategies to decrease the risk of HIV transmission to the baby
Two strategies to decrease the risk of hepatitis B transmission to the baby

parts_raw.text: 2 strategies to decrease the risk of HIV transmission to baby
2 strategies to decrease risk of HBV transmission to baby?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Intrapartum intravenous zidovudine now plus immediate maternal combination ART, with cesarean delivery considered and invasive obstetric procedures avoided. (2) Presumptive infant antiretroviral prophylaxis (zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine or raltegravir) started within 6 hours of birth, with no breastfeeding.
b) (1) Hepatitis B immune globulin to the infant within 12 hours of birth. (2) Hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth, completing the series at 1 and 6 months, with post-vaccination serology; maternal antiviral therapy with a tenofovir prodrug (which treats both HIV and HBV) further lowers maternal viremia.
questions.beyond_mandell: DHHS Perinatal HIV guidelines and CDC/PHAC hepatitis B perinatal recommendations — not covered in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: A) Start ART asap; IV ZDV during labor and until delivery if VL>1000; avoid invasive procedures; consider CS if VL>1000; start PEP for baby (ZDV+NVP+3TC x6 weeks); avoid breastfeeding. B) Maternal antiviral tx; HBIg at birth (within 12h); HepB vaccine at birth (within 12h) followed by dose 2 and 3 at 1 and 6 months respectively.

questions.question: A patient with compensated cirrhosis and genotype 1a hepatitis C needs treatment. He has HIV on tenofovir/emtricitabine (Truvada) and efavirenz.
questions.question_raw:
Q21 (2015)
Patient with compensated cirrhosis, Genotype 1a Hep C. Needs treatment. Has HIV on truvada/efavirenz.

parts.text: What viral test is needed if the patient is to start simeprevir/sofosbuvir?

parts_raw.text: Last question - what is viral test needed if patient to start simeprevir/sofosbuvir.

questions.model_answer: Test for the NS3 Q80K polymorphism. Q80K is present in about 40% of genotype 1a isolates and confers low-level resistance to simeprevir; it adversely affects response when simeprevir is used for short durations or in patients with cirrhosis, so if Q80K is detected an alternative regimen should be chosen.

cohort_answer.text: Check for Q80K polymorphism, confers low level resistance to in vitro simeprevir activity. If the patient is NON-CIRRHOTIC -> this does not matter. Can treat for 12 weeks. If the patient is CIRRHOTIC and Q80K polymorphism present, consider a different regimen. As a rule -> if patient has cirrhosis, we have to check for resistance. If the patient is not cirrhotic resistance testing is not usually needed.

questions.question: A patient with HIV is pregnant and is not on treatment.
questions.question_raw: A patient with HIV is pregnant. She is not on treatment:

parts.text: Name three antiretroviral regimens, and when would you start them?
What two recommendations do you have for the mother at delivery?
What regimen for the baby, and timing?
When would you test the baby?
Two current Canadian recommendations for feeding?

parts_raw.text: Name 3 antiretroviral regimens and when would you start them?
b. What 2 recommendations do you have for the mother at delivery?
c. What regimen for the baby and timing?
d. When would you test the baby?
e. 2 current Canadian recommendations for feeding?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Dolutegravir + abacavir/lamivudine (HLA-B*5701 negative only). (2) Dolutegravir + tenofovir (TDF or TAF)/emtricitabine. (3) Ritonavir-boosted darunavir + tenofovir (TDF or TAF)/emtricitabine. Start as soon as possible — pregnancy favours immediate initiation and earlier suppression means lower transmission risk.
b) (1) If the viral load is >1000 copies/mL, scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks with intrapartum IV zidovudine; if suppressed, vaginal delivery is acceptable. (2) Avoid invasive procedures — artificial rupture of membranes, fetal scalp electrodes, forceps or vacuum.
c) Start within 6 hours of birth: zidovudine alone for 4 weeks if the mother was suppressed on ART; presumptive three-drug therapy (zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine or raltegravir) if the mother was untreated or not suppressed.
d) HIV nucleic acid (DNA/RNA) testing — at birth (high-risk), 14–21 days, 1–2 months, and 4–6 months, with confirmatory testing of any positive result; antibody testing is not diagnostic in infancy because of transplacental maternal antibody.
e) (1) Exclusive formula (replacement) feeding is recommended in Canada, where safe replacement feeding is available. (2) Avoid mixed feeding; if a virally suppressed mother chooses to breastfeed after counselling, support her with exclusive breastfeeding, maintained maternal suppression, and close infant monitoring.
questions.beyond_mandell: Infant prophylaxis, diagnostic testing schedule and CPS/DHHS infant-feeding guidance are from the DHHS Perinatal guidelines and the Canadian Paediatric Society statement; not in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: a) Dolutegravir/Abacavir/Lamivudine; TAF/Emtricitabine plus dolutegravir (or TDF); TAF/Emtricitabine plus Darunavir/ritonavir (or TDF, better studied). Start ASAP. b) VL>1000: C-section at 38 weeks and intrapartum zidovudine. VL<1000: delivery mode determined by OB, consider intrapartum zidovudine. Avoid artificial rupture of membranes, forceps/vacuum extractor, fetal scalp electrodes. c) Presumptive therapy at birth with Zidovudine, lamivudine + nevirapine or raltegravir. d) HIV NAT at birth and 6 weeks. e) Exclusive formula; no mixed feeding (solid/liquid foods prior to 6 months increases HIV transmission risk).
